title: The Visitor of Marrow Creek
premise: Ada Vane, a meticulous property surveyor who has spent his life keeping people at arm's length, arrives in the dying village of Marrow Creek to appraise Hollowell House, a manor whose measurements refuse to stay the same. He learns the village has been paying a tithe to the house since 1911, when the church bell was melted down and its voice given to the walls; in 1974, the last bell-keeper stole the house's ledger heart and vanished with it, and the house has been starving ever since. As the harvest moon nears, the house begins claiming villagers to feed its hunger, and Ada realizes his own arrival was orchestrated: he is the stolen ledger's descendant and the only one who can return what was taken. In the climax Ada descends into the house's bell-well, offers the ledger heart back, and chooses to let the house take his name instead of his life, ending the tithe; he leaves Marrow Creek alive but unnamed, finally belonging to no one and no place, which is its own strange freedom.
about_author: Gideon Zhou is the pen name of a former land registry clerk who spent eleven years cataloguing properties that no one would buy twice. He writes horror from a rented flat above a decommissioned fire station, and claims his best ideas arrive whenever the building's old alarm tests itself at 3 a.m.

chapters.title: The Measurement Problem
chapters.summary: POV Ada. Ada arrives in Marrow Creek to appraise Hollowell House and finds every room measures differently on a second pass. The estate agent, Mrs. Tallow, is oddly eager to close the sale. Emotional beat: professional unease masked as professional pride.

chapters.title: A Village That Won't Look at Him
chapters.summary: POV Ada. The pub empties when Ada mentions the house's name; an old woman presses a iron nail into his hand and says 'count your doors.' Emotional beat: the loneliness Ada has cultivated curdles into something like being watched.

chapters.title: The Bell That Wasn't
chapters.summary: POV Ada. At dawn a church bell rings, though the parish records and a melted stump in the churchyard prove the bell was cast down in 1911. Ada photographs the empty tower; the photos show a rope moving. Emotional beat: rationality beginning to crack.

chapters.title: Ledgers and Long Teeth
chapters.summary: POV Ada. In the house's cellar Ada finds a tithe ledger listing names and payments in teeth, hair, and years of memory, ending abruptly in 1974. His own name appears on the last page, in fresh ink. Emotional beat: dread of being already claimed.

chapters.title: Mrs. Tallow's Confession
chapters.summary: POV Mrs. Tallow. The agent admits the village hired Ada not to sell the house but to be appraised by it; every surveyor before him stayed, or didn't. Emotional beat: betrayal, and the awful relief of finally being wanted for something.

chapters.title: The Bell-Keeper's Daughter
chapters.summary: POV Ada. Ada tracks down Edith Crane, daughter of the 1974 bell-keeper, who reveals her father stole the ledger heart—a bell-shaped core of the house's memory—and fled with it, dooming the village to the house's growing hunger. Emotional beat: grief for a father she never understood.

chapters.title: Doors, Counted
chapters.summary: POV Ada. The house begins rearranging itself at night; a door that led outside now leads to 1911's kitchen, warm and occupied. Ada nails the iron into the threshold and counts eleven doors where there should be ten. Emotional beat: claustrophobic vigilance.

chapters.title: The First Tithe
chapters.summary: POV Edith. The house takes the pub landlord, who walks into the fields at the bell's call and doesn't return. The village, ashamed, does nothing. Edith decides to give Ada her father's letters. Emotional beat: complicity and shame.

chapters.title: Letters from the Bell-Well
chapters.summary: POV Ada. The letters reveal the bell-keeper's plan: the heart must be returned willingly by one of his blood, or the house will take it back along with everything it can reach. Ada is the bell-keeper's great-nephew. Emotional beat: the trap of inheritance.

chapters.title: What the House Remembers
chapters.summary: POV Ada. Wandering the house's deeper rooms, Ada experiences its memories: the 1911 casting, villagers singing the bell's voice into the walls, the first tithe. He begins to feel the house's hunger as his own. Emotional beat: seductive dissolution of self.

chapters.title: The Harvest Moon Roster
chapters.summary: POV Mrs. Tallow. The village elders draw up a list of who will be given to the house if the moon rises with the heart unreturned. Ada's name is first. Emotional beat: cold arithmetic of a community preserving itself.

chapters.title: Edith's Refusal
chapters.summary: POV Edith. Edith burns her father's letters rather than hand over the heart's location, blaming the village for letting her father be the one to carry the theft alone. Ada must find the heart without her. Emotional beat: righteous anger hardening into isolation.

chapters.title: The Room That Appraises Back
chapters.summary: POV Ada. Ada confronts the house directly in its surveyor's study, where it measures him: his debts, his estrangements, the years he made himself small to stay safe. The house offers him belonging in exchange for the heart's location. Emotional beat: temptation of being truly seen.

chapters.title: Nineteen Seventy-Four
chapters.summary: POV Ada. A door opens onto the night of the theft; Ada walks into the memory and watches the bell-keeper pry the heart from the bell-well, hearing his own name called in the man's voice. Emotional beat: inherited guilt made flesh.

chapters.title: The Nail Comes Loose
chapters.summary: POV Ada. The house breaches Ada's wards; his rented room in the village inn folds into the manor's east wing. Villagers who once ignored him now beg him to hurry. Emotional beat: fear giving way to reluctant responsibility.

chapters.title: Edith's Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Edith. Edith reveals she kept one page of her father's letters: a map of the bell-well sewn into her childhood quilt. She gives it to Ada not for the village, but so her father's choice can finally mean something. Emotional beat: forgiveness as an act of will.

chapters.title: Descent
chapters.summary: POV Ada. On the eve of the harvest moon, Ada enters the bell-well beneath the house, past strata of tithes—names, teeth, wedding rings—while the walls whisper offers of every belonging he ever refused. Emotional beat: terror and terrible clarity.

chapters.title: The Heart of the House
chapters.summary: POV Ada. In the well's chamber Ada finds the heart's empty cradle and the house's true face: not a monster but a village's bargain, grown monstrous through neglect. It shows him the 1974 theft from its own wounded memory. Emotional beat: pity for the thing he must appease.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: POV Ada and Edith. Edith arrives at the well's mouth with the heart itself, hidden for fifty years inside the church's melted bell stump. The house's hunger surges up the shaft as the moon rises. Emotional beat: desperate race against the sky.

chapters.title: The Tithe of a Name
chapters.summary: POV Ada. Ada returns the heart, but the house demands payment for fifty starving years. He offers the one thing the ledger shows he has guarded all his life: his name, his identity, his place in any record. The house accepts. Emotional beat: sacrifice as the price of finally giving something away.

chapters.title: Silence in the Tower
chapters.summary: POV Edith. At moonrise the bell rings once, whole and resonant, then never again. The house goes still and ordinary, its doors all leading outside. The villagers emerge, ashamed and free. Emotional beat: hollow, hard-won relief.

chapters.title: The Surveyor Unnamed
chapters.summary: POV Ada. Ada completes his appraisal of Hollowell House—fair market value, no anomalies—and leaves Marrow Creek. Asked his name at the county office, he finds the page blank where it should be, and smiles. Emotional beat: eerie peace; belonging to nothing, and therefore to no one's hunger.
